chapter_title: Concerning the Dragon with Fourteen Heads; what it

6.original: [and reveal its likeness and its observation above and below, it wages war by]
6.content: and reveal its likeness and its observation above and below, it wages war by

fills.fill: in a mystery, and in purity
fills.notes: The substrate contrasts literal monstrous imagery with an interior (spiritual) teaching. “Virginity” here is the correspondential state of unmingled reception (unadulterated truth). The phrase needed is a fixed pairing: mystery/purity rather than exhortation.

fills.fill: because it was spoken in parable
fills.notes: The Magi are said to miss the inner sense; the natural segue is that the utterance was in a veiled form (parable/riddle), hence their literalism.
The surviving letters “spiri” constrain the completion. The clause’s function is to reclassify the written words as belonging to an inner register.
The sentence requires a verb of correspondential explication: the earth/dragon image “is interpreted” (not physically exists).
Bridges: “this earth … to it” and then “as it is accounted a corporeal dragon”. The point is likeness/correspondence between earth/body and dragon-image.

fills.fill: in the mystery of the body
fills.notes: The speaker promises instruction; the ‘dragon’ is immediately identified as doctrine/thought bound to flesh. A phrase marking the interior ‘mystery’ of embodiment fits the oldest-layer register.

Next clause: “the dragon is this doctrine … of the flesh”. The dragon is not ‘flesh’ itself but the mental/impulsive doctrine of the body; “thought” is later explicit in ¶7, so it fits as a forward echo.
Needed as a small connective to yield: “the dragon is this doctrine of the thought which is in the flesh …”.
After listing sight/sound/scent, the tongue is singled out; the missing phrase must identify its function in ultimates: tongue → speech (and then taste-selection).
The text totals fourteen by pairing seven ‘above’ with seven ‘below’. This lacuna must introduce the second heptad without shifting into moralizing.
“The seven of the torso are these: two …” The natural first pair on the torso are the hands/arms as instruments of action (effects).
To make paired ‘below’ members corresponding to action and locomotion; hands/feet are the most stable correspondential pair for outer powers.

A ‘ruler’ in the torso section points to the belly/appetite governing the outer members in the opposite sense (concupiscence). This yields: “the two … ruler … the seven heads that are above” → the lower appetitive rule over senses.

fills.fill: and reveal its likeness and its observation above and below, it wages war by
fills.notes: Accepting the provided reconstruction: it matches the substrate’s mechanistic description—through the ‘dens’ the dragon manifests and operates via the fourteen heads (faculties). No later devotional overlay.
“kills it in them …” requires a locative: the conflict is internal, within one’s own organs/powers (members), matching ¶6’s dens and ¶8’s ‘through them’.

The closing: “It does through them … / its des]ire all the time.” The intended sense is continuous operation through organs according to will/desire. Restoring a balanced pair “will … desire” fits the oldest-layer psychology.

assessment: Most gaps are structurally constrained by the chapter’s fixed correspondential scheme: dragon = thought/doctrine of the body; fourteen heads = upper seven senses plus lower seven bodily powers; five dens = inner organs. Exact wording in ¶2–¶3 and ¶5 is less tightly constrained (multiple equivalent formulae exist in this register), so those restorations remain tentative/moderate, while the ‘spiri…’ completion and ¶6’s supplied clause are strong.
